overview: A wet, unsettled pattern builds from Sunday through midweek. Storms move in off the Pacific and favor the Sierra and Cascades first, then the Rockies by Tuesday and Wednesday, with cold air and snow levels dropping behind each system.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: A series of systems arrives Sunday and runs into midweek, with gusty southerly winds and snow above about 7,500 feet. The forecasters are increasingly confident in this wet pattern. Kirkwood looks like the strongest spot, with Sunday the biggest day, and the NWS discussion notes gusts of 40 to 55 mph over the Sierra crest.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: Showers and mountain snow arrive from the Pacific in a series of lows, with the second system bringing widespread precipitation Sunday and Monday. Snow levels fall, and the most snow likely falls on Monday. Mt. Bachelor is the top pick, with Monday the biggest day, and Mt. Baker sees snow on Tuesday and Wednesday.

regions.title: Eastern Sierra
regions.text: Strong gusty winds arrive Sunday ahead of a storm, with gusts over the Sierra ridges reaching 80 mph or more. Valley rain and mountain snow follow, and snow levels drop sharply Monday night into Tuesday as a second low drops in from the north. Mammoth's biggest day is Tuesday.

regions.title: Southern Rockies
regions.text: A strong cold front brings hazardous winds Saturday, then a system moves into the Rockies midweek. The NWS in Albuquerque says rain and snow return to western and central New Mexico Wednesday and Thursday. Wolf Creek sees snow showers Wednesday, its peak day.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Showers and rain dominate the Coast Mountains through the week, with snow mostly confined to higher terrain. Cypress Mountain gets its biggest day Monday, while Whistler sees mostly chances of showers. Environment Canada's forecast is mainly rain at lower elevations.

ahead.text: The Climate Prediction Center expects above-normal precipitation across much of the Lower 48 for December 3 to 7, with a persistent western trough.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 25, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Dec 6–12. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
